column1: What did Jay Forrester identify as the biggest impediment to progress?
column2: Not the engineering side of industrial problems but the management side - social problems are much harder to understand and control than physical systems.

column1: What does the Forrester quote imply about engineering's role in a wicked problem?
column2: Engineering is part of a solution but can never be a complete solution.

column1: What was the Project on the Predicament of Mankind?
column2: A late 1960s / early 1970s report from the Club of Rome, an early group of intellectuals including Donella Meadows.

column1: What realisation prompted the Club of Rome report?
column2: That people needed to zoom out from their reductionist focus on specific problems and look at the whole planet.

column1: What is the lesson of re-reading the Club of Rome report 50 years on?
column2: The predicament has not got any better, and it shows just how little we listened.

column1: What does Jason Hickel's Less Is More show?
column2: That we keep restating the same problem decades later.

column1: What is New Zealand's complexity Centre of Research Excellence?
column2: Te Punaha Matatini, housed in Auckland with researchers around the country.

column1: Which institute was one of the earliest to address complexity as a subject in itself?
column2: The Santa Fe Institute.

column1: Why is no systems thinking book a method you can just apply?
column2: Because there is no one way to solve these problems - the books give ways of thinking about the puzzle, not parts of it.

column1: What reading is set for this course?
column2: At least the first two chapters of Thinking in Systems by Donella Meadows.

column1: What is the recommended way to prepare for the team project?
column2: Read Thinking in Systems - ideally the whole book, and ideally with a couple of people per team who have really delved into it.

column1: Name the five reading goals for Thinking in Systems.
column2: Hone your ability to recognise systems and their parts; look for interconnections; ask "what if" questions about future behaviours; be creative and courageous; and think about system design and re-design.

column1: Name the four waves of systems thinking in order.
column2: Hard systems, soft systems, critical systems, and universal or zoomed-out systems.

column1: Which wave of systems thinking is correct?
column2: None - it is an evolution, and depending on your problem any of them could move you forward.

column1: What does pluralism claim about problems?
column2: That there is more than one way of seeing a problem, both ways could be true, they may be incompatible, and the conflict may teach you something about the system.

column1: What are heuristics, and what is their risk?
column2: Quick mental shortcuts to reach an answer - sometimes helpful, sometimes diverting when the underlying assumptions are wrong.

column1: What does DSRP stand for?
column2: Distinctions, systems, relationships and perspectives.

column1: What does VMCC stand for in building an adaptive organisation?
column2: Vision, mission, culture and capacity.

column1: What is the culture test in the VMCC model?
column2: Whether it is safe to say you completely stuffed up and wasted two months, and ask how to prevent it - rather than hiding the mistake.

column1: What does VUCA stand for?
column2: Volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous - though the lecture's version reads volatile, uncertain, complex, uncertain, volatile.

column1: Why did Juliet change the VUCA acronym?
column2: She added an extra volatile because the world is getting more volatile, not less.

column1: Name the five drivers of the VUCA future.
column2: Technology, globalisation, demographics, climate change and geopolitical conflict.

column1: What does every new technology need, according to the lecture?
column2: Critical thinkers to figure out how to harness it to do more good than harm.

column1: What risks does globalisation create alongside its benefits?
column2: Huge global inequity and a lack of social cohesion.

column1: Give the worked example of VUCA drivers converging.
column2: A global supply chain dependent on the Strait of Hormuz, plus geopolitical conflict and volatile Western leadership, producing an unexpected war, blocked supply chains and fuel price spikes.

column1: Why does AI-driven warfare reduce the chance of diplomacy?
column2: Sending boots on the ground takes time and skin in the game; with AI, your AI fights my AI and we have blown each other up before anyone has time to think.

column1: What is the sting in the drones and AI example?
column2: Both risks were well documented when they emerged and the convergence was foreseen - and it did not stop it happening.

column1: Define a wicked problem.
column2: An issue that resists a complete or simple solution; it can likely be ameliorated but not solved, and the amelioration measures may create new problems.

column1: How does a wicked problem differ from a complex problem?
column2: A complex problem is hard but may have an optimal solution; a wicked problem cannot be solved.

column1: How does a wicked problem differ from a long problem?
column2: A long problem is defined by its timeframe; many wicked problems are both complex and long.

column1: What five adjectives describe wicked problems on the slide?
column2: Unsolvable, undefinable, unverifiable, unique and uncertain.

column1: Name the three axes of the wickedness triangle.
column2: System complexity, knowledge uncertainty, and stakeholder value divergence.

column1: What is the risk with any solution to a wicked problem?
column2: It probably will not solve it, may make it better, but is likely to have made something else worse - within your system or someone else's.

column1: State the system test.
column2: A system must have elements, connections and a purpose.

column1: What is an emergent property?
column2: Where the whole is more than the sum of the parts - a property emerges from the system that was not present in any of the parts.

column1: What is another word for a system's purpose?
column2: Emergence.

column1: What four things will a system have?
column2: Interconnected related elements, inputs, outputs, and a purpose.

column1: What happens the moment you draw a system boundary?
column2: The boundary is slightly arbitrary, and you immediately create tensions between the system you defined and the surroundings you influence but excluded.

column1: What are the two axes of the Head matrix?
column2: Increasing complexity of problems, and increasing difficulty regarding stakeholders and institutions.

column1: Name the three levels of the complexity axis in the Head matrix.
column2: Both problem and solution clear; problem clear but solution not clear; neither problem nor solution is clear.

column1: Name the three levels of the stakeholder axis in the Head matrix.
column2: Co-operative or indifferent relationships; multiple parties each with only some of the relevant knowledge; multiple parties conflicting in values and interests.

column1: Name the nine cells of the Head matrix.
column2: Tame, communicatively complex, politically complex; analytically complex, complex, politically turbulent; cognitively complex, conceptually contentious, and very wicked.

column1: What defines a very wicked problem on the Head matrix?
column2: Complex issues involving many stakeholders with conflicting requirements.

column1: Where do ENGGEN 303 and ENGGEN 403 sit on the Head matrix?
column2: 303 sits bottom left with tame problems; 403 sits top right with very wicked ones.

column1: What moves a problem to the right on the Head matrix?
column2: Adding more parties who disagree or hold only part of the knowledge.

column1: What moves a problem upward on the Head matrix?
column2: Losing clarity about what the problem is or what the solution would be.

column1: Name the four levels of the iceberg model, top to bottom.
column2: Events, patterns, structures and mental models.

column1: Which iceberg level is above the waterline?
column2: Events - what is seen from the outside.

column1: Define the events level of the iceberg.
column2: The level at which we typically perceive the world, such as waking up one morning to find we have caught a cold.

column1: Define the patterns level of the iceberg.
column2: Below the event level, where we notice that similar events have been taking place over time.

column1: Define the structures level of the iceberg.
column2: Below the pattern level, where we ask what is causing the pattern we are observing.

column1: Define the mental models level of the iceberg.
column2: The attitudes, beliefs, morals, expectations and values that allow structures to continue functioning as they are.

column1: Work Juliet's cold through the iceberg model.
column2: Event: a cold. Pattern: colds follow all-nighters and a night at the pub. Structure: poor time management, an overwhelming job description, workplace habits. Mental model: leaving things until the last minute.

column1: How does the levels of thinking model differ from the iceberg?
column2: It has more layers, and you can label those layers - for example technology, governance, business and market, and patterns of behaviour.

column1: What is the attitude to take toward these framing models?
column2: It does not really matter how you do the thinking - they are tricks to start conversations and organise your thoughts.

column1: What did Juliet do the first time she drew the levels of thinking model?
column2: She drew it upside down - offered as proof that it does not matter.

column1: Build the obesity iceberg from event to mental model.
column2: Event: obesity rising. Pattern: poor nutrition and limited activity. Structure: food deserts. Mental model: market forces dictate the food supply.

column1: What alternative framing was offered for the top of the obesity iceberg?
column2: Poor health outcomes - described as totally valid.

column1: What deeper causes sit under "market forces dictate food supply"?
column2: Heavily processed foods being cheap and abundant, and fresh food being sold at export prices and unaffordable locally.

column1: Where in the iceberg model do problem statements come from?
column2: The pattern level.

column1: What did Juliet do about limited activity in the obesity example?
column2: She parked it, choosing poor nutrition for her problem statement, and noted you might need two problem statements instead.

column1: What is a food desert?
column2: A place where there is hardly any fresh food - only cheap, heavily processed cupboard food.

column1: Why is obesity framed around food environments rather than self-control?
column2: Because it is not that people have no self-control - it is about the environment they live in, at the community level.

column1: Where does New Zealand rank for obesity?
column2: Third most obese country in the world, with a worsening trend.

column1: Which guide does the obesity example reference?
column2: Public Health England's "Whole systems approach to obesity" guide.

column1: Name the systems thinking tools taught in this lecture.
column2: The iceberg model, levels of thinking, trend maps, system models both conceptual and computational, leverage points, causal loops and feedback loops.

column1: What is a trend map used for?
column2: Looking at what is happening over time and whether there is repetitive behaviour or repetitive fluctuation.

column1: Name three questions to ask when exploring a system.
column2: What happened; what recurring events are we noticing; and what length of time is long enough to see patterns in systems function.

column1: Why is "what length of time is long enough" an important question?
column2: Because we are very good at seeing patterns, and the window may be too short for the pattern to be real.

column1: What is the key intervention question in systems thinking?
column2: Where in this system could we make small shifts that would make a big difference - and what trade-offs and unintended consequences exist.

column1: Give the methane example of unintended consequences.
column2: Eliminating New Zealand's methane emissions would mean removing dairy cows from Canterbury - with severe consequences for that economy and those people.

column1: In Meadows' list, which number has the least leverage and which the most?
column2: 12 has the least leverage and is closest to the system; 1 has the most.

column1: What is leverage point 12?
column2: Constants, parameters and numbers - such as subsidies, taxes and standards.

column1: What is leverage point 11?
column2: The sizes of buffers and other stabilizing stocks, relative to their flows.

column1: What is leverage point 10?
column2: The structure of material stocks and flows, such as transport networks and population age structures.

column1: What is leverage point 9?
column2: The lengths of delays, relative to the rate of system change.

column1: What is leverage point 8?
column2: The strength of negative feedback loops, relative to the impacts they are trying to correct against.

column1: What is leverage point 7?
column2: The gain around driving positive feedback loops.

column1: What is leverage point 6?
column2: The structure of information flows - who does and does not have access to information.

column1: What is leverage point 5?
column2: The rules of the system, such as incentives, punishments and constraints.

column1: What is leverage point 4?
column2: The power to add, change, evolve or self-organize system structure.

column1: What is leverage point 3?
column2: The goals of the system.

column1: What is leverage point 2?
column2: The mindset or paradigm out of which the system - its goals, structure, rules, delays and parameters - arises.

column1: What is leverage point 1?
column2: The power to transcend paradigms.

column1: Where are most real interventions designed, and why?
column2: At the shallow leverage points - they are easier to design around, easier to understand, and their impact is visible.

column1: What is the trade-off with deeper leverage points?
column2: They have higher transformative impact but are much harder to design for.

column1: Give an example of an intervention at leverage point 12.
column2: An EV subsidy of five or ten thousand dollars per car - some impact, but small.

column1: Give an example of an intervention at leverage point 6.
column2: Real-time electricity pricing, so you see the cost rise as you turn the heater up.

column1: Give an example of an intervention at leverage point 2.
column2: Making New Zealand a non-car-oriented society within a generation - a paradigm shift.

column1: Why can't a paradigm-level intervention be incremental?
column2: Because doing it within a generation cannot be iterative - adding more bike lanes will not shift the model that says cars are normal.

column1: What is the key skill of systems thinking, per this lecture?
column2: Understanding when and where you can pull levers.

column1: What is a balancing loop?
column2: A negative feedback loop where one element increases another which then decreases the first - goal-oriented, keeping the system in check.

column1: Give a physiological example of a balancing loop.
column2: Body temperature regulation.

column1: What is a reinforcing loop?
column2: A positive feedback loop where each element increases the other, so the system is always increasing - a runaway system.

column1: What is the relationship between B and R loops in a real system?
column2: Systems have a balance of both.

column1: How does a causal loop differ from a feedback loop?
column2: A causal loop is a more advanced form that adds positive and negative signs to each link.

column1: Explain the school discipline causal loop.
column2: Sending disruptive students to the principal leads to suspension, which reduces disruption for others - a balancing loop. But suspended students spend more time out of class, fall behind academically, find it harder to focus and act out more - a reinforcing loop.

column1: What does the school discipline example demonstrate about wicked problems?
column2: That an intervention which balances one loop can drive another - amelioration measures creating new problems.

column1: What causal loop map was shown for a national crisis?
column2: A map of how COVID impacted society, covering policy interventions, the financial and economic systems, the environment, individual wellbeing and society.

column1: Why are robust systems hard to disrupt?
column2: Because of resilience, self-organisation and hierarchy.

column1: How do you intervene in a robust system?
column2: By identifying leverage points or causal loops to impact.

column1: How detailed does a system map need to be?
column2: Not very - you can start literally on a whiteboard.

column1: What three questions do you ask while mapping a system?
column2: What do we know, what are we measuring, and what could we push on.

column1: What do you look for once the system is mapped?
column2: Which loops are amplifying the system, which are balancing it, and which loop dominates.

column1: Where is the point of impact in a system?
column2: Whatever dominates the system.

column1: What is the one-line warning about systems thinking as a method?
column2: Systems thinking is not an algorithm or a single process.

column1: What is systems thinking, according to the summary slide?
column2: An approach to broader understanding, critical thinking, and proposing interventions and solutions.
